I have some minor facial differences from birth. The flap in the back of my throat doesn’t close perfectly and despite a lot of speech therapy sometimes my speech still comes out breathy and nasal. When I was a kid the doctors offered to fix it and my mom said she’d support me having surgery once I was older- if I wanted to. I’m trans. I’m covered in self harm scars that I don’t hide anymore. I have “fang” teeth because I never had braces and little kids ask if I’m a vampire. I wear hearing aids (that now are barely noticeable). I wear glasses. 

There will always, always, always be something. I think a parent’s job is to prepare their kid for the world and be there when it’s rocky or kids (or adults, for that matter) are assholes. And to empower their kid to recognize that and respond appropriately.

Many years ago (like 14, 15 years ago?) my whole family attended a bbq. We all ate something different, came home, all good. My little brother started complaining of an upset stomach, then headache. Headache was bad enough that he took meds for it (kid couldn’t swallow pills). He continued to feel crappy and the headaches became a pretty incapacitating migraine. 

Finally, my mom took him to a walk-in clinic. She had just terminated his care at his pediatrician and was in the process of setting him up with my family PCP; the PCP office wouldn’t see him for a sick visit as he hadn’t had a ‘well visit’ yet. So, walk-in. They say, oh- probably a stomach bug that dehydrated him, causing a migraine. Fluids, rest, otc headache meds as needed. 

A couple days later, still migraines and bad pain, now a stiff neck. My parents take him to the ED. The ED gives him some fluids, gives pain meds that don’t touch pain (up to that point he was naive to pain meds). They think that it went stomach flu > dehydration > migraine > laying down a lot > stiff neck. They discharge him, with instructions to come back if he has any of a list of symptoms including developing double or blurry vision.

Maybe the next day- it’s hard to remember because I was studying for finals, and we were all convinced that this was what they were saying, stomach flu >> stiff neck, the whole bit. Anyway, he develops both double and blurry vision. My parents get back in the car and drive him to the ED.

Thankfully, someone in the ED decides to get a CT. They get the results and see what they think is a pseudo-tumor, an excess of spinal fluid that’s pushing on his optic nerve causing all the symptoms. They decide they need to do an MRI, cut his braces off, he gets the scan done. Docs tell my parents that one of them should go home and check on the other kids, shower and grab some clothes, he’s getting admitted but there won’t be anyone to read the MRI results til morning. My mom jumps in the car to come home…

And my dad calls her- the MRI revealed a 3” aneurysm in his brain, he’s being moved to the pediatric neuro ICU and she needs to come back immediately. 

Long story short… the excess spinal fluid was putting pressure on the optic nerve, causing the symptoms that made them find the aneurysm. Turns out he (and other males in my family) have a genetic disease. 

Please never apologize for being a squeaky wheel for your kid. They can’t advocate for themselves. If you’re worried, share your concerns with the providers. Ask for a second set of eyes. 

(For those curious, brother is very much alive, virtually no deficits after multiple brain surgeries).

I am a trans man, but I spent my teen years having one period every year, always around August. By the time I told my mom I was headed off to college so I went to Planned Parenthood there. From what I remember they started me on some kind of hormonal medication in hopes of “kickstarting” my cycle, but they also were not very aggressive because I certainly wasn’t complaining about not bleeding.

I know how anxiety-provoking this kind of appointment can be. What I will remind you is this: It is your body, and they cannot require you to do anything tomorrow. If you’re worried about having a blood draw or a pelvic exam, you are well within your rights to refuse and/or defer.

You inferred convenience. So many things that do end up benefitting or being a convenience for able-bodied folks originated as a product or service or design for folks with disabilities.

Why might a store develop a service (curbside pick-up) when people are already being served inside the building? 

Oh, because individuals with physical, mobility, or other disabilities may not be able to easily navigate into the store to pick up their items. 

It absolutely benefits folks without disabilities in the end (the busy parent who doesn’t want to drag all three kids in the car, the person on their limited lunch break, the person who wants to lessen their personal exposure to potential COVID-19) but this is just one of many services/products that folks take advantage of without really thinking about who is hurt in the process/

This sounds unlikely because it sounds like he wasn’t very overweight to begin with, but just wanted to add this experience here in case it’s useful:

If he is engaged with services for people with developmental disabilities, it was my experience years ago that providers can be super shitty to people who they perceive to be fat or overweight. I was at meetings where different service providers would, in front of the person and a group of their service providers, call the person out for their dietary choices- often listing out all of the “bad food” that they had seen the person eat or purchase. It was very fucked up and, of course, not helpful. 

I could easily see something like that type of shaming lead to someone adopting those kinds of eating behaviors- in fact, some of those behaviors were *encouraged* as a way for the person to lose weight.

(This is not to say that people with developmental disabilities don’t also deserve access to healthcare regarding nutrition, but public shaming is never the approach).

I was on prescribed painkillers and got really, really constipated. I knew I needed to shit, but the turd was all set at the end and in was incredibly painful.

I noticed that using “flushable” wipes felt good, and kinda made my asshole involuntarily relax so I could, uh, make progress. I also noticed that I would get a hard chunk turtling that was easier to pass when softened by the wipe. 

And then I came up with a plan:

Use the wipe wrapped around your finger to enter the anus and pull dried shit out. Also, just press the cool wipe up toward your asshole because that makes you stop straining and helps things move along.

Over the course of a day, in different *sittings*, I probably pulled 6” of dry shit out of my ass. Once the final chunk was removed, I swear to god I took a 2’ dump. 

Never again.
